newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: INTERVIEW - Portuguese firms pressured as EMU looms.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Portuguese firms pressured as EMU looms.

text.p: Portuguese companies are facing increasing competitive pressures as Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) looms and many will have to modernise to survive, Employment Minister Maria Joao Rodrigues said.

She told Reuters in an interview that the planned EMU membership would enable Portugal to join a stable economic framework that offered attractive conditions for investment such as low real interest rates.
But she added: "There are risks to take into consideration because competitive pressures will increase. In reality they are already increasing."

"The country has to prepare itself quickly so that its companies can adapt themselves to these new competitive conditions. We know that this adaptation is already happening," she said in the interview on Friday night.

Asked if low-wage countries such as those in Eastern Europe could lure foreign investment away from Portugal, she said: "I think this risk is relatively limited because Portugal now presents good conditions for attracting foreign investment.
"In 1996 we had a major influx of foreign investment."

The minister said that well-qualified Portuguese labour could be recruited at competitive salaries compared with other EU states and Portugal already had well-developed infrastructure such as telecommunications.
But she warned of low-wage Asian competition to traditional local industries such as textiles and clothing.
"Portugal will have to restructure its companies in these sectors to bolster their competitiveness -- not by cutting salaries, but by using new technologies better," she said.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres was offering incentives to help companies to modernise by encouraging them to recruit and train well-qualified people.

Rodrigues said she expected the Portuguese unemployment rate to remain fairly steady this year. "Macroeconomic forecasts lead us to believe that unemployment could remain stable in Portugal and could stand at 7.2 or 7.3 percent," she said.
Unemployment in the fourth quarter of 1996 was 7.2 percent.
Rodrigues said Portugal's economic recovery, its progress in boosting exports and the general upturn of the world economy would prevent a deterioration in the unemployment rate in 1997.

Portugal had unemployment compared with other European states because it had a low birth rate, people were staying in the education system longer and it had a relatively high proportion of women in the workforce, she said.

A possible reduction in EU development funds from 1999 would cut jobs in Portugal. "If the EU funds were reduced after 1999 this would bring, without doubt, bad consequences for employment prospects in Portugal," Rodrigues said.

EU funds received since Portugal's entry to the European Community in 1986 have been spent on building infrastructure, such as telecommunications and roads, high-technology investments and improving education, she said.

Rodrigues estimated that EU development funds had directly created tens of thousands of jobs per year in Portugal over the past decade. Public investments including EU funds had maintained 350,000 jobs in Portugal per year.
Rodrigues expected jobs to be created in services, car, electronics and paper industries, and to be lost in textiles, clothing, food and fisheries in the coming years.
